claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure featuring multilevel chemical fluctuations.
A hybrid physics-informed machine-learning workflow can predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness for HfNbTiVAl10.
The workflow integrates hierarchical-microstructure descriptors with first-principles outputs.
Elastic constants, misfit volumes, surface energies, and unstable stacking-fault energies are accessible using first-principles simulations.
The machine-learning algorithm should be trained on an experimental database encompassing multiphase and heterogeneous microstructures.
The workflow is intended for room-temperature tensile and fracture-test conditions.
The workflow assumes that the tested hierarchical heterostructure is statistically represented in the calibration data and remains stable during processing and testing.
Local bond distortion and chemical environment can be represented by effective misfit volumes and localized elastic-anisotropy metrics.
These local descriptors mediate Young’s modulus and yield strength at the continuum scale and fracture toughness at the defect-nucleation scale.
Machine learning can correlate descriptors sampled from representative microstructural regions with global mechanical-property outcomes.
Sampling only representative regions reduces dependence on full high-fidelity simulations of the entire heterogeneous structure.
The workflow will predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness within 5–10% of experimental measurements.
The workflow will reduce computational time or resource use by a factor of 5–10 relative to conventional DFT/CALPHAD approaches.
The workflow will improve prediction accuracy by approximately 5–10% relative to existing machine-learning or phenomenological models.

Direct DFT evaluation of alloy fracture or yield strength is generally beyond currently available implementations, and first-principles calculations for disordered multicomponent alloys remain challenging.
Ab initio and molecular-dynamics methods are time-consuming, while CALPHAD can require significant computational resources.
Existing phenomenological models typically provide 70–90% accuracy for strength-related metrics.
The workflow may become unreliable when phase transformations, chemical ordering, degradation, or fluctuation length scales fall outside the training domain.
Fracture-toughness accuracy and transferability to uncalibrated temperatures or loading conditions are more uncertain than in-domain predictions.

A blinded prospective benchmark will falsify the hypothesis if errors consistently exceed 10% or the workflow fails to achieve at least a fivefold efficiency gain under stable-microstructure conditions.
